title: Umm Ayman
hookLine: the woman who nursed the baby Muhammad ﷺ, whom he called my mother after my mother

lines: AS THE PROPHET USED TO VISIT.
cards: Two leaders of Medina walk to the house of an old woman. One is Abu Bakr, the new leader of the community. The other is Umar.
The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, has died, and Abu Bakr says: come, let us visit Umm Ayman, the way the Prophet used to visit her. They knock. They sit with her.
And she begins to cry. Before we hear why, it helps to know who she was, and why the Prophet kept going to her door. Today: Umm Ayman.

teach.b: Her name, tradition says, was Barakah. A note in Sahih Muslim, from the early scholar Ibn Shihab, describes her plainly.

teach.h: SHE CARED FOR THE BABY MUHAMMAD.
teach.b: She came from Abyssinia, served in the household of Muhammad's father, and after his father died she looked after the baby until he was grown. She was the mother of Usamah.
Nursed here means cared for and carried, not breastfed; his milk-mothers were other women. So yesterday's young commander was her son, and Zayd was her husband.
Tradition says that when Muhammad's mother died on a journey, it was Umm Ayman who brought the little boy home, and that years later he would say of her: she is my mother after my mother.
That line comes from the biographies, so hold it as the tradition's memory. What Muslim records firmly is the visit.

teach.h: ABU BAKR AND UMAR VISIT HER.
teach.b: Abu Bakr and Umar come to her house after the Prophet's death. She weeps, and they try to comfort her. Don't you know, they say, that what is with God is better for His Messenger?
And she answers: I know that. That is not why I am crying.

I am crying because the revelation from heaven has stopped. Her answer moved them to tears as well, the report says, and they wept with her. The woman who carried the baby is the one who understands what has ended.
The leaders came to comfort her, and she ended up teaching them. And they came because he used to come. Honoring the woman who raised him did not end with his death.
It went on, through a visit.

how: Muslims remember Umm Ayman as the Prophet's nurse and the mother of Usamah, and retell the report in Sahih Muslim of Abu Bakr and Umar visiting her after his death.

o: the woman who cared for the baby Muhammad
the Prophet's birth mother, who died on a journey
his milk-mother among the desert tribes

p: visited her as the Prophet used to
the revelation from heaven had stopped

s: Umm Ayman wept because she doubted the Prophet was with God
she said she knew what is with God is better for him. she wept because revelation had stopped.
Abu Bakr and Umar wept with her
Muslim's report says her answer moved them to tears.
the line 'my mother after my mother' is recorded in Sahih Muslim
it comes from the biographies; Muslim records her care for him and the visit.

games.q: you are Abu Bakr, newly leading the community after the Prophet's death. there's an old woman he used to visit. what do you do?
o: send her a gift through a messenger.
go to her house, with Umar, as he used to.
invite her to come to you.
games.why: Muslim reports Abu Bakr said: let us visit Umm Ayman as the Messenger of God used to visit her. and she ended up teaching them.

practice: Bring to mind someone who looked after you when you were small, or sick, or new somewhere, maybe not a parent, maybe someone the world didn't call family, and remember one specific thing they did.
Say thank you to them in your mind. If they've died and you pray, you can ask mercy for them.

wordCard.voice: Umm Ayman. The woman who nursed and cared for the baby Muhammad, mother of Usamah, visited by the Prophet and, after him, by Abu Bakr and Umar. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: 'mother of Ayman', a name taken from her son Ayman.

carryVoice: Your line: my mother after my mother. The visits went on after he was gone. Day eight hundred thirty, done.

sources.ref: Sahih Muslim 2454 (Abu Bakr and Umar visit Umm Ayman; she weeps that revelation has stopped)
Sahih Muslim 1771 (Ibn Shihab's note: Umm Ayman, mother of Usamah, an Abyssinian servant of Abdullah ibn Abd al-Muttalib, looked after the Prophet until he was grown)
Ibn Sa'd, al-Tabaqat al-Kubra (her name Barakah; 'my mother after my mother')
